As soon as we get the planning permission and the survey done. I think we’re going to do a bit of a modern twist on the place. Make it a bit more open and light. That sounds good – but I hope you’re not going to turn it into some kind of modern art gallery. We don’t want to lose the character of the house. Absolutely not, Mum. We just want to keep it cozy and functional. Maybe even add a new kitchen and some storage space. That would be great. I’d be happy to help out if you need any ideas or even just a few hours of manpower. Oh, we’d love that. It’s a bit of a project, but it’s going to be worth it. And speaking of projects, have you found a place for the new garden shed yet? Not yet, but I’ve got a few ideas. Maybe we can put it next to the garage. I think it would make things a bit easier for storage. That makes sense. I think it would be better to keep the garden as open as possible, though. You know, for the kids to play in. Oh, we’re not worrying about the kids anymore, but I do enjoy having a bit of space for the garden.

So, do you know what’s up with this catfish thing? I saw this video on TikTok where someone was trying to catch a catfish in a pond, and it was  so  dramatic. Like, they were screaming and throwing things into the water, and the catfish just swam away like it didn’t even care. Oh yeah, I saw that! My cousin tried to do it too last summer. He said he was going to “do a real man thing” and fish for a catfish, but he ended up just getting his feet wet and stepping on a frog. Haha, that sounds like a  real  adventure. I mean, I’ve only ever seen catfish in videos. I don’t even know if they’re real. Like, do they actually live in ponds or are they just some kind of myth? They’re real, I think. I’ve seen them in rivers before. But they’re not the easiest to catch. They’re pretty big and strong, and they don’t like being handled. I once saw someone trying to fish one and it just bit through the line and pulled the whole rod out of the water. Oh no, that sounds like a nightmare. I’d rather just watch Jeremy Kyle and then laugh at how dramatic he gets. I swear, he’s like a version of himself on a show. Like, he’s got this way of making everything sound like a huge deal when it’s just a normal argument between two people. Yeah, I mean, his show is a bit of a mess. I remember one episode where he was talking about a couple fighting over a tea towel. Like,  literally  a tea towel. I mean, I get that people have arguments, but come on, this is going too far. I know, right? I mean, it’s kind of funny to watch, but it’s also just so over-the-top. I think he’s just trying to make drama for the cameras. But then again, he does have a way of making people feel like they’re being understood, even if they’re being ridiculous. Yeah, I think it’s partly the audience he’s going for. Like, if you’re someone who’s had a bad day or just wants to cry, his show is like a safety valve. But for the rest of us, it’s just like, “Why is this man still on TV?”

So, do you remember the first time we went to Paris together? I still can’t get over how beautiful it was, and how everything just seemed to flow so smoothly. Oh, how could I forget? It was the summer after you finished your degree—your first real break. I was in the middle of a residency, and you showed up with a suitcase full of books and a laptop, completely lost but excited. I had to save you from getting too confused by the metro system. Yeah, I remember! You had to draw a map on the back of a café napkin. I still have that. It’s covered in little arrows and notes, like a children’s drawing. Oh, it’s still in my studio. I keep it framed. It’s a reminder of how far you’ve come, and how much you’ve grown. You were so eager to learn, even back then. I still remember how you spent hours in the Louvre, in awe of the art, and then later, how you got into a debate about the Mona Lisa with a group of tourists. I had no idea what I was talking about, but I said it like I knew everything. You were so proud of me. I think that’s why you always encouraged me to study Classics. You said it was important to understand the past, and how it shapes the present. Exactly. And you did it. You studied Latin, Greek, and even German. For a moment, I thought you’d become an academic. But then you changed your mind and went into computer science. I was a bit surprised, but I supported you. Yeah, I had to. My family didn’t really understand why I wanted to study something so “difficult.” But you were the first one who believed in me. You know, I still barely speak German now. I think I’ve forgotten most of it. That’s okay. You don’t need to speak it perfectly to appreciate it. And you know, I still speak it better than you ever did. I could hold a conversation with a native speaker without breaking a sweat. I guess I’ve been focusing more on code than translations these days. But I still find myself thinking about Italy sometimes—especially when I’m working on a project about ancient Rome or something. That’s the spirit.

I can't believe we've been on the road for three hours already. I thought it would take less time. I know, I’m more used to driving in London. This is like a different world out here. You know, I remember when I first moved to Harlow, I thought I’d never get used to the open roads. It’s so different from the city. Yeah, I mean, I never thought I’d be driving into Dorset, but here we are. It’s like a trip back in time in some ways. I’ve been meaning to talk about this—what do you think about the new roadworks? I almost had an accident last week when I was trying to get onto the A33. I heard about that. I think the council is trying to make it look like a modern route, but honestly, it feels more dangerous than ever. I was just thinking about that. I saw some stats online earlier. There was a report about dangerous driving in rural areas—more accidents, more speeding, less enforcement. Right, and with all the new technology in cars, you’d think it’d be safer, but no, it feels like the opposite. I remember my son once told me he was almost rear-ended because the other driver didn’t know how to use the Sat Nav properly. I can believe that. I’ve had those days where I just don’t want to drive. I’d rather take the train, even if it takes longer. It’s not just the driving, though. I mean, what about the towns? I heard about some places in Dorset that are just… bad. Oh, definitely. There’s this one that I know of where the housing is a bit run-down, and the locals don’t really look after the place. I passed it on my way to Bournemouth once. I can see how that would be a problem. I always thought the countryside was such a beautiful place, but clearly, there are some parts that aren't as well maintained. I guess it’s a bit of a mix. I mean, I’ve been looking up some places to visit while I’m here. I think I might do a little holiday in the area. You should. It’s a great place for a break. Just don’t forget to check your MOT before you go.

I've been thinking a lot lately, love. Oh, really? What's on your mind, dear? It's just... these days, you know? The way things are changing so fast. I feel like I'm being left behind. I know, dear. I've felt the same. It's hard to keep up with all the new technology. I still don’t know how to use that new smart TV, and I don’t even want to know. Yeah, I remember when we had a black-and-white TV. You'd sit there, and it'd make that lovely little hum. Now it's all high definition, and I can't even tell if it's real or not. I know, I know. You'd think after all these years, we'd be more used to it, but we're not. It's like the world's moved on without us. And the kids these days! I saw a boy the other day, maybe eleven, playing with a tablet like it's the most important thing in the world. I couldn't help but think, "What did I do with my time?" I know, love. But maybe it's just the way it is. You know, we had our time, and now it's their turn. It's just... I feel like I’ve missed so much. When I was younger, I worked in the factory, and I had a good life. Then the factory closed, and I had to retire early. Oh, I remember that. I used to visit you when I was working, and we’d chat about the news and the weather. Now I just sit at home, looking at the sky and wondering what's going to happen next. It's strange, isn't it? I used to like the routine. I had a schedule, I had friends, I had a purpose. Now I just sit here, and I wonder if I’ve done anything worth remembering. You've done a lot, love. You raised a family, you helped so many people in the community, you were a good friend. You’ve lived a good life. I know, but I wonder if anyone even remembers me anymore. I feel like I’m just a footnote in the story of the world. No, no, no. You’re not a footnote. You’re a chapter. A very important one. I hope so, love.

So, do you know what’s been playing on repeat in my head all day? That new album by The National. It’s got this really jangly guitar sound, and it’s just so atmospheric. I feel like it’s got this kind of melancholy vibe, but it’s also really catchy. Yeah, I heard about that. I actually got it on Spotify last week. It’s not the most upbeat thing, but I think it’s got this kind of emotional weight to it. It’s like, you know, it’s not just music—it’s like a whole story. Exactly! I was thinking about how much I miss my old friends from university. You know, the ones who would just show up at my door with a guitar and a new album. It’s funny how time changes things, isn’t it? Definitely. I’ve been thinking about that too. I mean, we’re all in different places now. Some are still in academia, like me, and others have moved on to different careers. It’s a bit of a bittersweet feeling, like you’re still connected, but the context changes. Yeah, and it’s not like we don’t keep in touch. We’ve got this group chat, and we still talk about music, and random things. But it’s not the same as being able to just drop by someone’s house and hear them play something new. That’s true. I miss that kind of spontaneity. Although, I have to say, I’m not bad at gardening. I’ve been trying to grow some herbs in the back garden. It’s been a bit of a struggle, but I’m getting the hang of it. I think I’ve got some basil going now. Oh, you’re doing it? That’s great! I’ve been trying to grow some tomatoes, but they’re all just bushes. I think I’ve got the soil wrong. I’ve heard people say that the weather here in Cambridge is so unpredictable. One day it’s sunny, the next it’s raining like a waterfall. Yeah, I feel you. I always thought the weather here was more temperate, but it’s like it’s got its own mind. I’ve been trying to keep a garden journal, just to map out when things are blooming or not. It’s kind of a way to stay grounded, you know?

I just can’t believe how long it’s been since I’ve had a proper job. It feels like forever. I got offered a research position last week, but I had to decline because I was still waiting for a final decision on my PhD funding. It’s so frustrating, you know? Yeah, I get that. I’ve been in a similar boat. I’m still waiting on my thesis submission, and I’ve been working part-time just to keep afloat. It’s not easy, especially with the cost of living rising and university fees still hanging over us like a cloud. I know, it’s like we’re both stuck in this limbo. I mean, I’ve always been a bit of a workaholic, so not having a steady income is really hitting me hard. I’m constantly thinking about what I’m going to do after this. I just don’t want to end up like my dad, working in a warehouse for the rest of his life. That’s understandable. I remember when I first started university, I was so focused on getting through the courses and managing my finances, but now it feels like everything is catching up with me. I’ve even started thinking about teaching again, but I don’t know if I want to go back to that grind. Plus, I’ve got so much to finish with my PhD. I can imagine. I’ve been trying to keep myself busy by taking on some freelance projects, but it’s not the same as having a proper job. I miss the structure. Although, I have to admit, it’s given me a lot of time to think about what I really want from life. Maybe I should consider something more creative? That’s a good point. I’ve been thinking about the same thing. I’ve had this idea for a musical for a while now. Not like the big productions, just something small, something that I can write and maybe put on at a local theater. It’s been on my mind a lot lately. I think I need to give it some serious thought. A musical? That’s ambitious, but I can see why it’s calling to you. I mean, you’ve always had that spark for the arts. Even when you were in school, you were the one writing plays and putting on little performances for your friends.

Mummy, I’ve been thinking about making a picture book for our little brother. You know, like a story about our family. Oh, that sounds lovely, sweetheart. What would you like to include? I was thinking about our family tree. You know, with all our names and where we came from. Maybe even some pictures of us when we were little. Aye, that’s a nice idea. I’ve always loved family trees. They tell so many stories, don’t they? Yes, they do. But, love, you know your brother hasn’t even been born yet. How do you plan to include him? Well, I can draw him as a baby, maybe with a little hat and a teddy bear. And I’ll write about how he’ll grow up and go to school with us. That’s very thoughtful. I remember when I was teaching, I used to have the children draw their own family trees. It was a great way to learn about where they came from and who they were. I remember reading a book once about a family that had a storybook about their own lives. It was very touching. Maybe you could do something like that. Yeah, I want to make it special. Maybe with some pictures of our house, our garden, and even the park where we used to play. Oh, the park! That’s where we first met your father, wasn’t it? Though I’m not sure how that’ll fit into a children’s book. Well, maybe in the stories of the older brother or the stepsons. I mean, we all have different stories, don’t we? Yeah, I know. There’s a lot of different family styles. Some people have parents who are still together, some aren’t. Some have stepsons, like me. It’s all different. Aye, life’s full of different paths. But it’s the love that binds them all together, isn’t it? That’s true. And I think that’s what your book should show – the love, the stories, and the connections. I like that. Maybe I can go to the park tomorrow and take some pictures of the swings and the slide. They’ll go in the book. That sounds like a wonderful idea. And don’t forget to include the family dog, too. He’s part of the family, even if he’s a bit of a gremlin.

So, do you ever just get fed up with having to shave every day? I mean, it’s not like I’m doing anything special, but it’s just so much work. Honestly, I can totally relate. I feel like I’m always either shaving or thinking about shaving. It’s like my face is a battlefield every morning. Yeah, and it’s not even like I have a lot of hair. I mean, I have stubble, but it’s not like it’s some wild growth or anything. It just seems like the norm now. Maybe it’s just the way we’re raised. Like, we’re told from a young age that we need to look clean-shaven. But what if we just stopped? I mean, not that I would, but I’m curious. I guess I’ve always thought that shaving was just part of being a woman. Like, if you don’t do it, you’re not taken seriously in some circles. But I also feel like there’s this pressure to have a certain look, and I don’t even know why. I think it’s more about how we’re socialized. Like, if you don’t shave, people might think you’re lazy or not caring. But honestly, I just feel like it’s a waste of time. I could be doing something more useful with that time. Yeah, I get that. I mean, I do it because I don’t want to look like I’m going out with a beard. But I’ve been thinking about maybe just letting it grow a bit. Like, a little bit of stubble. It might be easier on my skin too. That actually sounds like a good idea. I’ve had a few friends who’ve gone the stubble route and they all say their skin is better. Plus, it’s less maintenance. No razor, no cream, no irritation. I guess I could try it. Though I’m not sure if I’d be ready to give it up completely. Maybe start with just a few days of not shaving and see how it goes. Yeah, that’s a good plan. It’s not like we’re going to be judged for a few days of stubble. Besides, if it doesn’t work out, we can always go back to the razor. Right. And who knows, maybe we’ll start a trend.

So, do you know what’s the biggest thing about the alphabet? I mean, it's such a basic thing, but it's kind of like the foundation of everything. I was thinking about it the other day, like, how do we even start to read without it? Honestly, I think it's kind of strange that we don’t use the alphabet in other ways. Like, in football, for example—do you ever think about how the players use the alphabet to avoid racism? I mean, some of them use their names to mask their ethnicity. It's a bit of a sad thing, isn't it? Yeah, it's a bit of a shame. I mean, I’ve heard about some players who go by initials or even change their names to protect themselves. But I guess it’s part of the game, right? I mean, the sport is supposed to be for everyone, but sometimes it’s not. Exactly. And it’s not just about the players, it’s also about the fans, the way they act towards them. I had a friend once who was a big fan of a certain team, and he would always make racist comments about the players from other countries. It was really disturbing. I tried to talk to him about it, but he just brushed it off. That’s so frustrating. I mean, it’s one thing to have personal opinions, but it’s another to act on them in a public space. I’ve heard that in some places, people still get away with it. It’s like a culture of ignorance, isn’t it? Yeah, and it’s not just in football. I think it’s all over the place. But I guess we’re starting to see more awareness now. I mean, the players are speaking out more, and fans are being called out for their behavior. It’s a slow process, but it’s happening. I agree. And it’s not just about politics. I think it’s also about education. If people are taught to respect others from a young age, maybe they’d be less likely to act that way. Though I’m not sure how much of a role education plays in that. Hmm, that’s a good point. But then again, sometimes people are just ignorant. I remember once, I was at a boxing match, and someone in the crowd was making fun of a fighter’s name because it sounded “foreign.”

I just got a call from the council about the request for funding for the old mill in Dorton. They’re considering it, but they want more specifics on how the project would benefit the local community. Oh, that’s interesting. I heard they’ve been looking for projects that combine preservation with public access. You know, the kind of thing that can really make a difference. I’ve been thinking about that. If we can show that the mill can be turned into a community arts space or something like that, it might hit the right notes. The council really values community engagement these days. That does sound like a solid angle. I’ve been working on a few similar proposals for other buildings. You know, the key is to not just preserve the structure but to ensure it has a future. Exactly. I’ve had some concerns, though. The structural assessment came back with a few issues that need addressing. It’s going to be a bit of a challenge to get the funding approved if we don’t have a clear plan. I know what you mean. I had a similar situation with that old bakery in Wotton. The original plans were great, but the budget didn’t account for some of the hidden costs. It almost cost us the project. Oh, I remember that. You were so frustrated. But I think you pulled it off in the end, didn’t you? Yeah, just barely. I had to revise the budget and work with a local architect to find more cost-effective solutions. It was a bit of a headache, but it worked out. Maybe we can do something like that. I’ve been talking to a few local architects, and one of them is interested in helping out. Maybe they could give us an estimate on the costs and suggest some alternatives. That sounds like a good move. And if we can involve the local community in the planning process, it might help with the funding approval. People love to be part of something that matters. Right. I’ve been thinking about setting up a small consultation group with nearby residents. They might have some good ideas, and it would also show the council that there’s real local support. I like that idea. You know, sometimes the best solutions come from the people who live the closest to the problem.

So, do you know what’s really interesting about the way people speak in different regions of England? I was reading this article the other day about dialects and how they’re changing, especially with the rise of digital communication and social media. It’s like we’re all kind of blending our accents now, or at least that’s what it seems. Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. I mean, I grew up in Birmingham, so I have that strong Midlands accent, but now I find myself using more of a Northern or even a Southern accent in different contexts. It’s almost like we’re becoming more linguistically flexible, which is kind of cool, but also a bit worrying. Exactly. I think it’s partly because of the way we interact with others online. You can’t really tell where someone is from just by their voice anymore. I mean, even my own accent has shifted a bit since I moved to Cambridge. I used to be more of a Sunderland accent, but now I sound more like a Cambridge academic. That’s funny. I feel the same. I was in a discussion group the other day, and I mentioned something, and someone asked me where I was from. I said Cambridge, and they said, “Oh, you have that nice, posh, Oxford accent.” I was like, “No, I’m from Birmingham.” And they just laughed and said, “Sorry, I don’t know any other accents.” It was a bit of a shock. I think that’s part of the problem—people don’t really differentiate accents as much anymore. It’s not just about where you’re from; it’s also about how you speak. I mean, even in my family, my mum has this really strong Northern accent, but she’s been living here for years, and she still sounds like she’s from Newcastle. I think it’s really hard to unlearn that. Yeah, and I think that’s part of what makes linguistics so interesting. It’s not just about the words you use, it’s about the way you use them, the rhythm, the intonation, and how all of that changes depending on your background. I’ve been studying this for my PhD, and it’s fascinating how much identity is tied to language. That’s so true. I mean, even our research at work deals with how language shapes identity, especially in multicultural settings.

Alright, let’s talk about the school dinners. I know the kids are getting really picky now. Emma, have you checked what they’re serving this week? Yeah, Mummy, I saw the menu. It’s chicken nuggets and peas again. I’m not eating that. I prefer real food, like sandwiches or something. I know, I told my mum I don’t like the school food either. It’s so boring. I’d rather bring my own lunch. That’s a good idea, but the school doesn’t allow packed lunches. They say it’s not fair to the other kids. I mean, I understand, but sometimes the meals are just not up to scratch. I know, Mummy. I asked my teacher about it, and she said they’re trying to get better meals in. But I still don’t like the way the food tastes. It’s all too salty. Yeah, I remember when I was at school, the dinners were terrible, too. I think the budget is tight, especially now with the cost of living rising. But we need to make sure the kids are getting proper nutrition. I think the school should have a better system. Maybe they could get a chef in or something. I saw a news story about a school in London that started serving better meals and the kids loved it. That’s a good point. Maybe we could talk to the headteacher about it. We’re in a position to help, especially with the school tennis tournament coming up. I mean, it’s not just about food—there are other costs too. Yeah, I heard about the tennis tournament. Are we going to take them? I don’t want to spend too much money on it. We’ll see. I’m trying to get some sponsorship from the local community. I know some people in the village who might be interested. Also, I think the school is offering some sort of financial support for families who can’t afford it. That’s good. We don’t want to miss out on the tournament. It’s a chance for the kids to have fun and meet other kids from the area. I’m a bit nervous about it, though. What if I get scared of the clowns again? I remember last year when we went to the circus, and the clowns made me laugh, but also a bit scared.

I just watched that new film about the 1960s. It was really interesting, but I couldn’t help but think about how different the education system was back then. Yeah, I remember reading about that debate in Cambridge last week. They were arguing whether history should be taught more in a narrative form or as a series of facts. I think it’s important to tell the story, not just list dates and events. I agree. I think the current national curriculum is quite rigid, especially for history. It feels like it’s more about memorizing dates than understanding the context. I remember when I was at school, we had to write essays and do projects. It made history feel more alive. That’s interesting, because I went to a school where we were encouraged to think critically about what we learned. We had to analyze sources and discuss different perspectives. It was a bit more challenging, but I think it helped us understand the subject better. I went to a school where we just learned the facts. There was very little discussion or debate. It felt like we were just being told what to think rather than being encouraged to form our own opinions. I still feel like I missed out on some of the deeper understanding of history. That’s probably why so many people – even those with degrees – feel confused about history these days. It’s not just about facts anymore. It’s about how history is interpreted and what it means for today’s world. I think the national curriculum needs to be more flexible and allow for more discussion. I think that’s what the debate was about. Some people think that the curriculum is too narrow and doesn’t prepare students for the real world. I mean, how do you apply historical knowledge to modern issues if you just memorize dates and names? Exactly. And then there’s the question of how to prepare for higher education. I think the current system is not well aligned with what employers are looking for. A degree is one thing, but how do you translate that into real-world experience? That’s a good point. I know a lot of young people are struggling to find work after university because they have degrees but no practical skills. I think there needs to be more of a link between education and industry.

I've been thinking a lot lately about the war, you know. It's been on my mind since the first tank rolled into the city. I can't stand to see the way things are going. It's like we're back to the old days, the days when things were simpler. I know, it's really unsettling. I remember when I was a child, the only wars we heard about were on the radio. Now, it's like every day there's a new conflict somewhere. It's just so chaotic. And the way the government handles it, it's like they don't care what happens to the people. I mean, I've seen enough in my time to know that when there's a war, the real cost falls on the common people. I agree, but I also think we need to be careful not to let fear take over. We've seen how fear leads to extreme measures, and that's never good. Exactly. I was just thinking about my grandfather, he fought in the war. He always said he never wanted to see another war, and he never did. But now, it feels like it's happening all over again. It's strange, isn't it? I was just talking to my daughter about how we're so much more connected now, but at the same time, we're more divided than ever. It's like the world is moving in two different directions. You're right. And with the way the media portrays things, it's easy to get confused. I've had to rely on my own knowledge and experience to make sense of it all. I think that's the key, isn't it? To question everything and not just take what you're told at face value. I mean, I'm in a position where I can afford to think about these things, but I know not everyone has that luxury. That's true. I can't imagine what it's like for people who are struggling just to make ends meet. When there's a war, the first thing that goes is the basics—food, shelter, safety. It's a real shame, isn't it? I remember when I was a child, my mother used to tell me about the war, how people had to share everything. It was a different time, but I think we're losing that sense of community.

So, do you think we’ll be able to fit all our stuff in the car? I feel like we’re already over the weight limit just with the boxes from the loft. I’d say we’re pushing it. I can’t even remember the last time I drove a car that full. But it’s all for the best, isn’t it? Moving out on our own is a big step. Yeah, I guess so. It’s just a bit weird, you know? I mean, moving out of Mum’s for the first time. I never thought I’d be the one saying goodbye to my childhood home. I know. I remember when I left home for uni, it felt like the end of the world. But you grow up, and one day you’re standing on your own two feet. Still, it’s not the same without her here. I know. She’s been so supportive through everything. Even when I was getting sick last month and couldn’t work for a week, she didn’t make me feel like I was a burden. She’s always been like that. Remember when you got that flu bug your first year at uni? She drove all the way from Bedford just to bring you soup and pills. You were barely conscious, and she was there for you. Yeah, I remember. It was the best thing. But I don’t know if I can handle this on my own. I mean, I’ve got the flat, the job, and everything, but it’s not the same as having her around. You’ll get used to it. You’re not alone, though. I’m here, and so is your sister. And you’ve got your own money now. You’re not a kid anymore. Maybe. I just worry about the mortgage and the bills. I’m not sure I can pay for everything on my own. What if something goes wrong? I know, but you’re not alone. We all have to help each other out. And when things get tough, just remember we’re not that far away. You can always come back here for a visit. That’s comforting. I just hope I’m ready. I’ve been thinking about the move for so long, but now that it’s actually happening, it feels like a big leap. It’s a big leap, no doubt.

Alright, do you think we've got everything for the birthday meal? I've been going through the list again just to be sure. I think so, but let's double-check. We still need to buy the fish, right? And the candles. Oh, and the table plan—should we print it out or just write it on the whiteboard? I think we should print it out so everyone can see it clearly. I've got the names sorted, and we’ll seat them by age, just to make sure the older ones are near the warmth. Although, I’m not sure how that’ll work with the dementia thing. Yeah, we need to be careful with her. She’s been forgetting things more lately, so maybe we should have someone sit with her during dinner to make sure she doesn’t get lonely. I’ll ask Aunty Ruth if she can help. That’s a good idea. I mean, she’s been in touch a few times, and she’s quite fond of her. I think she’d be happy to help. Also, I was thinking—should we try one of those Great British Bake Off desserts? Like a banana tart or something? That sounds nice. It’ll be fun to have something a little special. Though I’m not sure about the cake. I’ve got a bit of a sweet tooth, but the last time she had a cake, she tried to eat the candles. It was a mess. Oh, that was a disaster. I remember that. She was so embarrassed, and we had to buy new tablecloths. Still, it was a good laugh. I guess we should make sure the candles are safe this time. Maybe even use LED ones. Yeah, that’s a good idea. LED candles are safer and don’t smell as much. I’ll check the shop for some. Also, we need to make sure the fish is fresh. I called around, and the fishmonger said he can deliver it fresh this morning. Perfect. I’ll sort out the delivery details. Oh, and about the photographs. I’ve been thinking—we should set up a little photo corner with some chairs and a backdrop. It’ll be a nice way to capture the moment. I love that idea. It’ll make the day even more special. I’ll bring some props from the attic, just in case.

So, do you know what’s going on with my wisdom teeth? I’ve been trying to get an appointment with the dentist for ages, but they’re all booked up. I can’t even remember the last time I had a proper check-up. Yeah, I know, you were telling me about it on the train. I mean, I think they’re just waiting for you to develop an infection or something. You’ve been eating too much chocolate, haven’t you? Oh, come on, you know I haven’t been eating that much chocolate. I mean, I’ve been studying a lot, and when I do eat, it’s usually something like a sandwich or a cereal bar. Still, I can’t help but think about how much pain I’m going to be in when they finally take them out. I’d say you’re definitely going to be in pain, but maybe not as bad as when I had mine done. I mean, I had to be put under general anaesthetic and everything. It was like a dream for a few hours, but then I woke up with this massive headache. Yeah, I remember you talking about that. You said it was like having a hangover, only way worse. I can’t even imagine going through that. I just hope it doesn’t take too long. I’m not looking forward to having to eat solid food for a while. You know, I think I’m going to miss eating proper meals for a bit too. I mean, when I had mine done, I could only have soft foods for weeks. I remember eating soup and toast all the time. It was so boring, honestly. Yeah, I can’t wait to get back to normal eating. I’m just so tired of chewing everything. I mean, what’s the point of eating a sandwich if you can’t even chew it properly? Exactly! And I was just thinking about how I’m going to move house next month. I’ve got to start sorting out all my stuff. I’ve been meaning to get rid of some of the old stuff I don’t use anymore. It’s going to take forever to sort through everything. Yeah, I know you’re going through a lot right now. I mean, moving house is a massive job, especially when you’re still at university and everything.

Alright, so I was thinking about doing some random acts of kindness for Chinese New Year. Do you two want to help me out? Yeah, that sounds nice! What do you have in mind? I like that idea! I can help you make some things. Perfect! I was thinking of making lactose-free cakes and cookies for people who might be sensitive to dairy. I’ve been experimenting with some new recipes, and I think they’re going to be really good. That’s amazing! I love baking. Can I help with the frosting? Of course! And I also thought about using some old chess and draughts pieces to make money for a charity. I know you both have some old sets at home. Oh, I still have my set from when I was little. I didn’t know you could use them for that! How does it work? Well, I’ve seen some people selling them online, and I thought it could be a fun way to raise money for a good cause. I could set up a little stall at the local market or even sell them online. It’s a way to give back during Chinese New Year, which is all about community and generosity. That sounds like a great idea! I can help you set up the stall. I’ve done some market stalls before. I can help too! Maybe we can make some little tags with the pieces, and put them in a box. That way people can buy them as little tokens of goodwill. Exactly! And the money we raise can go to a local food bank or something like that. It’s a small gesture, but I think it can make a real difference. I love that. I’ve been thinking about doing something similar for my school project. Maybe we can share ideas? That would be great! I’d love to hear what you’re thinking about. And by the way, I was also thinking about dying my hair different colors for Chinese New Year. I’ve always wanted to try something bold. Oh, I’ve seen your hair before! You have such a cool style. You should try a bright color. Yeah, I’ve been considering it. Maybe something like pink or purple. I think it would be a fun way to celebrate. What do you think? I think you should do it!

Mummy, I just wanted to say… I think I saw you on the Internet yesterday. Oh, really? What did you see? I was looking up something about Alice in Wonderland, and I saw a photo of you in a green dress, like in the book. I thought it was a costume, but then I realized it was you! Oh, that was last year when we went to the theatre. I had a costume party and wore a green dress with a white bow. It was so much fun. Didn’t you want to come? I wanted to, but I was busy with school. I’ve been studying for my exams, and I’m so stressed. I know, darling. You’ve been working really hard. But don’t forget to take care of yourself. You’re still young, and there’s time to enjoy things like Alice in Wonderland and costumes. I know, but I also want to finish my exams and get into a good college. I’m worried about the future. I understand, but you’re not alone in this. You’ve got me, and I believe in you. Besides, if you pass your exams, we can go to the theatre together. I’ve already booked tickets for  Alice in Wonderland  next month. Really? That would be amazing! Yes, and we can even dress up like the characters. You could be the White Queen, and I’ll be the Red Queen. It’ll be like a real play. I’d love that! But… I’ve heard that people are scared of the theatre. Why? It’s just a play. You’re safe. I’ve been going to the theatre since I was a child, and it’s always been my favourite thing. Plus, you’ve always loved stories. Yeah, I do. I read a lot. My teacher said I have a good imagination. That’s why you’ll love it. You’ll feel right at home. And besides, I think it’s time you started thinking about what you want to do after school. You’ve got so many options. I know, but I’m not sure what I want to do. That’s okay, sweetheart. You don’t have to have everything figured out right now. Just take it one step at a time. And remember, I’m here to help you. I know. I just… I feel like I’m falling behind.

I just had a call from the solar panel group last night, they were really grateful for the advice we gave them. It was a bit of a brouhaha down at the council meeting, but we managed to put some of the finer points across. Yeah, well, you know how these things go. You've got the planners on one side, the energy companies on the other, and then the locals with their concerns. It's like a three-way tug-of-war. It's not just that. You've got the local government and their pockets tied up with the big energy firms. It's like they're all in cahoots. I've heard the council’s planning committee is being funded by a renewable energy company, which is a bit of a conflict of interest. I know, it’s absolutely disgraceful. And the way they’re handling the planning appeal is just a bit of a farce. You need to be well-informed and have a solid strategy, otherwise you’re just wasting your time. That’s why I think we need to do more research. Not just on the technical side—like how these wind turbines actually work—but also on the political angle. You’ve got to know who your allies are and who your enemies are. It’s not just about the wind power; it’s about the people and the money behind it. Exactly. It’s not just about the turbines or the solar panels. You’ve got to look at the bigger picture. Who benefits from renewable energy? Who gets the subsidies? And who ends up paying for the research? I mean, the Government spends a fortune on subsidies for wind and solar, but when it comes to energy storage research, it’s like they’re not even interested. Oh, I know. I’ve read some reports about it. They plug the gap with subsidies, but when it comes to the tricky bits like storage and grid integration, they’re not funding it properly. It’s all about short-term gains. And the Scottish referendum is just around the corner. I wonder what the implications are for the whole energy debate. If they vote yes, it could shift the whole political landscape in the UK. It’s a whole other layer of complexity. Scotland has its own energy policies, and it’s going to be interesting to see how this plays out in the wider UK context.

I just got a letter from the DVLA saying I need to renew my licence, and it’s reminding me that I haven’t driven in a while. I’m feeling a bit rusty, to be honest. Oh, I know what you mean. I’ve been meaning to get my licence back for ages, but I just haven’t found the right time. I think it’s about the same age as you, Dad. Oh, I remember when you were young, you were always pulling the car up to the kerb like a pro. Didn’t even need to think twice. You were a real driver back then. That’s what I tell myself, but now I have to worry about things like insurance, and all those new rules. It’s just so different from back then. I think it’s just the way things are now. I’ve been looking into taking lessons again, but I’m worried about the cost. I mean, with the cost of living rising, it’s not something I can just do on a whim. I can see that. But I think it’s worth it if you’re going to be driving regularly. And you know, with the holidays coming up, it would be nice to have a car again. Yeah, I was thinking about that. I’ve got a few family members coming over for the weekend, and I’d like to take them out for a drive. It’d be good for them to see the countryside again. That sounds like a great idea. I could help you with the insurance part. I’ve been looking at different policies for my own car, and I might have a few ideas. You could do that, love. I’d be happy to help too. I mean, I’m not exactly a driving expert, but I know how to fill out forms and talk to the insurance companies. That would be great. I’ve also been thinking about holidays. I was talking to my sister about maybe going to the coast again. She’s been wanting to take the kids out for a break. That sounds lovely. I’ve been meaning to visit my parents in Cornwall for a while now, but I’ve been so busy with work. I think I need to make some time for that. Cornwall is a beautiful place. You know, your mum used to go there every summer when she was younger.

So, Dad, I've been thinking about moving to Brighton. I've got this job offer, and it's really got me excited. The city is so vibrant, and I think it would be great for me to start fresh. Brighton, huh? You know, I remember when I was your age, I used to go there all the time for the races. Back in the 50s, it was a different place altogether. The beaches were cleaner, and the whole vibe was more laid back. That sounds amazing. I wish I could go back and experience that. You would, but it's not the same now. I've been keeping up with the news, and I hear that the cost of living is through the roof. Even basic things like parking are a nightmare. Yeah, and I heard the council is trying to implement some new parking policies. It's been a real pain for people who live in the city. It’s not just parking. I’ve noticed the way people are so caught up in their phones these days. They don’t even notice what’s going on around them. I mean, even your mother uses Facebook and gets notifications all the time. I know, it's a bit overwhelming. But I think it's part of modern life. Still, I can't help but feel like there's something missing. You're right. There’s a loneliness to it all. I used to cook up a storm, especially when the weather was nice. I’d make all sorts of dishes, like a proper Sunday roast with tea and biscuits. Oh, I miss that. I’ve been cooking more lately, but I don’t have the same routine. I try to keep the kids healthy, but it’s not always easy. Food banks are such a necessary thing now, aren't they? They are. And I think it's not just about the food. It's about the support system. I remember when I was working, I used to meet people from all walks of life. We shared stories, and it made a big difference. I think I need to start looking into some community groups. I’d like to get more involved. That's a good idea. You know, if you ever need help or just want to chat, I'm always here. And if you're ever thinking about moving, your mother and I would be more than happy to help.

So, do you remember that time we tried to act Shakespearean at uni? Oh yeah, we were so dramatic. I still remember you trying to recite  Macbeth  in a posh accent while pretending you were a 16th-century poet. Yeah, and then I slipped up and said “ Thou art a dastardly villain ” and looked at the coffee table like it was the Globe Theatre. You were so serious about it. I thought you’d actually join the Royal Shakespeare Company. I almost did. I had a bunch of brochures and everything. But then I realized I’d rather be playing golf than doing Hamlet. Fair enough. But you still think Shakespeare is the best thing ever, don’t you? Of course. He’s got that amazing skill of making people feel like they’re in a tragedy, even if they’re just talking about their weekend. You’re right. But I still think sarcasm is way more effective. Like, instead of going full Shakespeare, just say, “That’s the kind of thing you’d say in a play, but in real life, we just say ‘that’s ridiculous’.” Mate, you’re just trying to be smarter than me. No, I’m just being realistic. You know, I’ve been trying to learn how to play golf. Like, properly. Not just knocking a ball into a tree like a five-year-old. Yeah, I saw you the other day. You hit it so far it ended up in a bin bag at the back of the park. I didn’t mean to. I thought it was going to land in the water hazard. You’re not even trying. You should’ve just made up a nickname for yourself like “The Golfer Who Can’t Hit a Straight Shot.” That’s not funny. I’ve been working on my swing. I even got a coach. A coach? You’ve got a coach and you still can’t hit the ball? I’m not the only one. I bet you’re just as bad. Oh, I’m not. I’m actually pretty good. I might even win the local tournament. Yeah, right. You’re just trying to flex. You know what? I did win once. It was a casual game at the park. You were lucky. No, I was skilled. And I’ve been practicing. You’re still not convincing me. Fine, fine. I’ll just go and beat you in the next round.

So, how’s your week going? I’ve been swamped with event planning, like, constantly. I think I’ve booked out the entire calendar for the next two months. It’s exhausting, but I love it. You’re not the only one. I’ve been working 12-hour shifts on the construction site, and I’m still trying to get through the week. I’ve got this new job with a different company, but it’s the same old grind. It’s wild, isn’t it? I mean, I got my postgrad in management, but I still end up doing the same stuff as everyone else. I’m a production controller, but the real work still feels like it’s done by the guys on the floor. I hear you. I was always told I’d be in a high position because of my degree, but here I am, still managing events for a small company, and I’m working weekends just to keep up. It’s the same for me, honestly. I’ve got a degree in engineering, but I still end up doing the physical work. I guess it’s just the way it is. You’ve got to be practical. Yeah, but I mean, we’re all in this together, right? I’ve been thinking – maybe we should all just take a break, go on a weekend trip together. You know, like, get out of the city for a bit. There’s this place in the countryside, near Oxford, that I found online. It’s got a really nice pub and a few hiking trails. That sounds like a good idea. I’ve been meaning to get out more. I’ve been so stuck in the office lately. I’m not even sure if I can afford to go on a trip, though. I’m not sure I can afford it either, but I bet we could split the costs. Maybe we could do something cheaper, like a day trip. I heard there’s a new festival in Cambridge this weekend. I could meet you there? That could work. I’ve got a few things to sort out this week, but I think I can make it. I’ve also been thinking about trying a new diet. I’ve been on keto for a month now, and I’ve lost like five pounds. That’s amazing! I’ve been thinking about starting a diet too, but I can’t seem to stick with anything.

Well, I've just had a look at the sky, old man. That eclipse was a doozie. I got the kids to put on their sunglasses and we stood in the garden, just watching it all go dark. It was eerie, really. Looked like the end of the world, but it wasn’t. Just a bit of natural magic. I heard about it on the radio. They said it was the first time in a hundred years or something. I was going to go out, but my back’s been acting up. I’ve got this stiffness that won’t go away. I went out too, even though I’m not feeling great. I thought it would be worth it. It’s always nice to see something like that, even if you’re not in the best shape. I took some painkillers beforehand and I think it helped. That’s the spirit, lass. You never know when you’ll get another chance to see something like that. I’ve got to tell you, though, the way the light changed was something else. I’ve seen a lot of things in my time, but that was up there with the best. You know, I’ve been thinking about moving. The house feels too big now. I was looking at some small flats in the town. Maybe something with a garden, you know? You can’t have everything, but a little bit of green space is good for the soul. I’d say that’s a good idea. We’re all getting older, and it’s not just the body that needs a bit of space. The mind needs a break too. I’ve been thinking about starting a small veggie patch in my new place. Maybe even some herbs for the kitchen. Oh, lass, I’ve got a few plants in the garden. I’ve been trying to grow some tomatoes, but the weeds are getting the better of me. I should have started earlier. Still, I’m not giving up. It’s something to do, and it’s better than sitting on your backside all day. I know what you mean. I’ve been thinking of getting a few plants too. Maybe some lavender. My wife used to love that. She said it calms the nerves. I’ve been feeling a bit on edge lately, with all the uncertainty. It’s all about mindfulness, isn’t it?

So, do you know where we're going for dinner tonight? I was thinking maybe that new place near the station... the one with the good reviews? I’ve heard of it, but I’m not sure if it’s worth the hype. I mean, it’s a bit pricey for what it is, don’t you think? Well, I reckon it’s worth it if you like a bit of a change. I’ve been eating the same old stuff for ages. Plus, it’s got that little courtyard and the view of the river. It’s a nice spot. Yeah, I guess. But I’m not sure about the food. I’ve heard some people say the portions are too small. And then there’s the question of parking. The car parks there are always full. I know, I know. But I heard they’ve added a few more spaces recently. And if it’s too busy, we can always go somewhere else. Like that café on the High Street. It’s not fancy, but the food is good and the prices are more reasonable. That’s true. Although, I have to say, I’ve been to that café a few times and it’s always a bit crowded on weekends. You have to wait for a table. I know, but I think it’s better than nothing. I mean, the alternative is going out and eating takeaway, which I’m not sure I want to do every night. It’s getting old. Fair enough. But I was thinking, maybe we could try that new Japanese place that just opened up near the bus stop. It’s got a great reputation, and it’s close enough that we don’t have to worry about parking. Hmm, that sounds promising. I’ve heard some good things about it. But I’m not sure if it’s any good for vegetarians. I’ve got this terrible habit of eating meat every single night. Well, you can always ask the chef. I mean, it’s not like we can’t just order something that’s good for you. You know, a bit of variety would do you good. I suppose you’re right. I’m just getting a bit tired of the same old meals. I mean, I’ve been working late a lot recently, and it’s hard to find time to cook.

Mornin’, Eileen. You look rather chipper this morning. What’s got you in such a good mood? Oh, I’m just feeling rather sprightly today, Joan. I’ve been out in the garden this morning, feeding the birds, and the sun was shining bright. It’s been a nice change from the usual grey skies. That’s wonderful. I heard the birds singing so loudly this morning. Do you know what kind they are? I tried to figure it out. I think there was a goldfinch, a blackbird, and a sparrow. I’ve been trying to identify them more closely. I even got the bird guide out again. It’s like a bit of a hobby now, really. That’s a lovely hobby. I used to love birdwatching when I was younger. But then I got too busy with work and family. I still enjoy listening to them, though. They always seem to sing at the same time, like they’re having a little concert. Oh, I know what you mean. I’ve noticed that the birds start singing earlier in the spring. It’s a sign that the weather is getting warmer, isn’t it? I always feel a bit more cheerful when I hear them. Definitely. I was out this morning, and I had the window open. The sound was so soothing. I even got up early to hear them. I blame the alarm clock for that, though. It was just too loud. That’s the thing with alarm clocks, isn’t it? They’re meant to wake you up, but sometimes they’re louder than the birds! I’ve had a few friends who’ve complained about their alarms being too loud. One even said it gave her a nosebleed! Oh, that’s not nice. I had a nosebleed once. It was after I’d been out in the sun too long. I thought I was going to be a goner for a moment. I had to sit down and calm myself down. That sounds awful. I remember hearing about a friend of mine who had throat cancer and it was related to constant coughing. I hope you’re all right now. I was fine, thank you. It wasn’t anything serious. I just had to be careful with the sun. I suppose it’s a good thing I’m getting older and more cautious. I’ve been thinking about gardening more lately, though.

So, how have you been? It’s been ages since we last caught up. I feel like we’ve both had so much going on lately. Oh, I’ve been good, thanks. Just been trying to keep up with life. You know, being a single parent is a constant juggling act. I’ve been thinking about how much things have changed since we were at university. I remember that time when we were just trying to survive on takeaway and barely had time to study. Now, you’re a social worker and I’m a teacher—both of us in the same socio-economic bracket, but with very different lives. Yeah, it’s weird how things turn out. I’ve actually been thinking about changing careers again. I’m so burnt out, and I feel like I need something new. It’s not just about the job, though. It’s about the lifestyle. I miss the freedom of being able to travel and not worry about deadlines. That’s understandable. I’ve thought about writing a book too. I mean, I’ve always loved stories, and I’ve had so many experiences as a teacher—some really inspiring, some quite heartbreaking. It might be a way to process everything. That sounds amazing. But I also know how hard it is to get started. Have you ever tried to write anything before? I’ve dabbled in some short stories, but I haven’t really taken it seriously. I keep putting it off. Speaking of time—have you ever thought about using social media to promote your writing? I’ve seen some people do it successfully. Honestly, I haven’t. I’m not really into social media. I mean, I use it for work and to stay in touch with friends, but I don’t think I’d ever use it to promote myself. I always thought it was a bit of a hassle. I used to feel the same way, but I’ve started using Instagram more. It’s not for the whole world, but it helps me connect with people who might be interested in what I do. Plus, it’s made me rethink how I present myself to others.

So, do you know, I’ve been thinking a lot about education lately. It’s such a strange thing—how much it changes, and how it affects people’s lives in so many ways. Oh, I know. I’ve spent my whole life in education, you know. Teaching for thirty years, then retiring. I’ve seen it all, really. Some of the best and some of the worst. That’s incredible. I mean, I’m a language teacher, so I get to see it from a different angle. I work with young people, helping them develop their skills. It’s rewarding, but also exhausting. I can imagine. You know, when I was teaching, I always believed in the power of education to change lives. But these days, I hear so many stories about how it’s not accessible to everyone. Especially for people like me, now that I’m retired and not working, it feels like I’ve been left behind. That’s true. I think there’s a huge divide now. People who have the means to continue learning—whether through courses, books, or online resources—have an advantage. But for others, especially those without stable incomes or support, it’s harder to keep up. Absolutely. And it’s not just about formal education. I mean, I’ve got a postgraduate degree, but I’ve had to rely on my wife to support me through the years. I’m not sure what I’d do if I didn’t have someone looking out for me. That’s a big concern, isn’t it? I mean, with the cost of living rising and more people struggling to make ends meet, it’s hard to see how people without jobs or savings can even afford to learn new things. It’s terrible. I’ve also been thinking about the younger generation. Some of them are so optimistic, so driven, but others are just giving up. I remember one of my students a few years ago—really smart, but he was so stressed about money that he couldn’t focus on his studies. It broke my heart. That’s heartbreaking. I’ve seen similar things in my classroom. Some of the students come in with so much potential, but they’re just too overwhelmed by the pressures of life outside school. I think we need to find better ways to support people, especially those who are struggling.

So, do you know what’s on the agenda for tomorrow? I think we were supposed to meet up at the café near the university, but I haven’t heard back from anyone yet. Yeah, I saw the message. So, do you think we should go to the gym tomorrow? I’ve been trying to get back into shape and I feel like I need some motivation. I’m with you on that. I’ve been wanting to get out of the city for a bit. I think camping or going somewhere with nature would be great.

I can't believe the amount of money they're paying for that striker. I mean, he's only been on the team for a couple of months, and already they're talking about a £50 million move. So, do you remember when we first brought the boys home from the hospital? It was such a busy time. I remember the first time they came to visit us in Ireland. They were both so little, and we had to keep them entertained all the time. Oh yes, I remember that. They were both so curious about everything. I think they were just fascinated by the Irish countryside. And that time when we took them to the fun fair in Cork – they were both so excited about the rides and the games. Oh, I still remember when the boys were little and we went to the cinema for the first time. They were so scared of the dark, but once the lights went out, they were like little kids in a movie. I still laugh about the time one of them screamed so loud that the whole theatre turned around. Oh, I had the same experience with my own grandchildren. They’re just like the ones you have, but they’re even more energetic. When I took them to the London Marathon, they were both so proud of their dad. I remember that one of them even wanted to run with him, but he said no, it was too far. They still talk about it. Yeah, and I remember how much they loved Iceland when we went there. The Northern Lights were amazing, and they were so fascinated by the natural beauty there. I think that trip really bonded them as a family. And don’t forget the birthdays. Every year, they had such fun. I think the best one was when we took them to a theme park. They were both so excited, and they spent the whole day being happy. It was such a joy to see them so content. I remember the time when the boys were teenagers and we had to take them to the cinema. They were so into their own world and couldn’t stop talking about their friends. I found it really hard to keep up with their conversations. But now, they’re older, and they’re starting to think about their own futures. It’s amazing how time flies. I still remember when they were born, and now they’re all grown up. It’s such a privilege to be part of their lives. I think the photo book is a great way to remember all the good times we’ve had together.

So, do you remember when we were kids and we used to play that game with the wooden blocks? The one where you had to build a house and then knock it down? I think it was called ‘It’s a Small World’ or something like that. Oh yes, I remember that! We used to use the old blocks from the shed, and we’d build these elaborate castles. My brother used to be the king, and I was the princess. I think we even had a tiny bed for the prince made out of cardboard. Oh, I remember that too. I think I was the one who made the bed! And we used to dress up in the old clothes from Grandpa’s wardrobe. It was so much fun. I still have some of those clothes tucked away in the attic. That’s so sad. I think I still have a couple of those blocks. They’re pretty worn, but I’ve kept them since childhood. I used to think they were the best ever. I wonder if they even still make them. I don’t think they do. They probably use plastic now. But I remember one time we had a competition to see who could build the tallest tower. I think it was something like three feet high. We had to use all the blocks, and my brother won because he just piled them up, whereas I tried to make it look like a real house. Silly boy! You were always too meticulous. And you used to get so frustrated when the blocks didn’t fit together properly. I used to just pile them up randomly. It made a much more interesting shape, if you ask me! I guess it’s all about different styles. I actually think the way you used to build those blocks is something I still do when I’m trying to make something. I love the way they fit together, even if it’s just for fun. I still do that too. I actually started knitting again recently. It’s kind of like building with blocks, but with yarn. I found some old patterns from my mum’s stash, and I’m making a blanket for my niece. That sounds lovely. I used to knit a lot when I was younger. I even made a cardigan for my daughter. It took me weeks, but she absolutely loved it.

I've been thinking, you know, about the old days, when we used to go down to the coast and fish. It was a different time, wasn’t it? Oh yes, it was. I remember when we'd set off in the early mornings, the sea was so calm, and we'd catch mackerel and herring. We didn’t have all this fancy gear now, just a net and a boat. Yeah, and the fish were so big. I used to think, "How can we eat all of this?" But now, when I see the fish in the shops, they're all small and look like they've been kept in a tank. It's like everything's changed, isn’t it? The way we live, the way we work, the way we eat. I used to say to the kids, "You won’t know what it's like to work hard, because we worked hard." That's true. When I was younger, I used to work in the fields. We'd start at five in the morning, and by the time we got back, it was dark. I don’t think I’ve ever had a proper holiday in my life. I know, I used to say the same. But you know what? Even though we didn't have much, we were happier. We had each other, and we had our home. That’s what I always say. We might not have had the money, but we had the togetherness. These days, people just run around, always on their phones, never stopping. It’s sad, really. I remember when we used to sit out in the garden with our tea and talk about everything. Now, even the kids don't want to sit and chat. They just want to be on their devices. I know. My grandkids come over, and they’re always looking at their screens. They don’t even notice the sun going down. It's like they’ve forgotten how to enjoy the little things. I suppose it's just the way of the world. But I still think that the best things in life are the simple ones – a good meal, a nice cup of tea, and a chat with someone you love. Exactly. And I think that’s what we’ve got here. We’ve got each other, and we’ve got our sandwiches. What could be better than that?

So, how’s the new job going? You mentioned you were going to start teaching again, right? Yeah, it’s been a while since I’ve been in a classroom. I think I’m doing part-time at a local primary school, teaching English and literacy. It’s a bit of a change from my previous role, but I’m enjoying it. That sounds great. I’ve always wanted to be a teacher, but I ended up going into copywriting. It’s a different kind of creativity, but I guess it’s still creative in its own way. I can’t imagine doing anything else. I love working with kids. I mean, the chaos is part of the fun, right? My classroom is always a mess, but it’s so rewarding when they finally get it. I know what you mean. I had a student last week who was really struggling with reading. I spent the whole lesson working with her, and by the end, she was reading a book on her own. It was incredible. That’s amazing. It’s those little moments that make it all worth it, isn’t it? I think about teaching all the time, even when I’m at work. I was even watching a documentary about education last night, and it got me thinking about how much we can influence people. Totally. I mean, the English language is such a big part of that. You know, I’ve always been fascinated by the way people use language. Like, sometimes it’s so different from how it was a hundred years ago. Yeah, and with technology, it’s changing even faster. I mean, I remember when people used to write in long, complex sentences. Now, it’s all short texts and emojis. I guess it’s a generational thing. Exactly! I mean, it’s kind of both nature and nurture, isn’t it? The way people speak and write is influenced by their environment, their upbringing, and the culture they’re part of. I think that’s true. I’ve noticed how my family uses a lot of slang and regional expressions, even though we’re all from different parts of the UK. My mum’s from Bristol, my dad from London, and my sister from the South of England. It’s like our own little dialect mix. That’s funny. I’ve noticed that too.

So, do you live close to the school, Sarah? I mean, I know it's in Liverpool, but I'm curious how far you have to walk or drive to get there. It's not too bad. I live about ten minutes away, so I catch the bus most days. It’s not the most scenic route, but it gets me there on time. Oh, I’ve been thinking about moving closer too. I’ve got this flat in the city centre, but I’m worried about the rent. My parents are helping me out, but it’s still a big chunk of my salary. Yeah, I know what you mean. I live in a council house about a mile from the school, but I still feel like I’m always running late. My mum says I should get a car, but I’m scared of driving. That’s a bit of a dilemma, isn’t it? I mean, I used to live in the same area as you, Sarah, and I always thought the commute was too long. But once I got used to it, it became part of the routine. I can see how that would be. But then again, there’s something about living close that makes it easier to just walk around. I’m just starting out in my career, and I feel like I’m constantly juggling responsibilities. I’m also trying to get into a better job, but the opportunities here are limited. I hear you. My dad’s always saying I should get a part-time job to save up for uni. But I don’t really want to work during term time. I’m trying to balance my studies with my social life, and I’m already stretched thin. I get that. I mean, I’m not in school anymore, but I still feel the pressure to be responsible. Especially when it comes to my son. He’s getting older, and I don’t want him to feel like I’m not there for him.

So, I heard you mentioned Nepal again. That’s a long time coming, isn’t it? I mean, you’ve been talking about it for months now.      Oh, it's been on my mind for ages! I’ve even started looking at flight deals. But it’s not just the flights—there’s the accommodation, the guides, and the logistics. I’m dreading the packing. I’ve got a list of things I need to bring, and I swear I’ve got a drawer full of gear that’s never been used.      That’s the worst part, isn’t it? I’ve got a friend who went to Nepal with a suitcase full of hiking gear and left it all in the hotel. She came back with a new set of clothes and a camera.      Ha! I’ve been thinking about that. I remember she was so excited about the photos she took, but then she said she never got to see them in the light.      Oh, I remember that. She took the photos, but she couldn’t even get the batteries to work. She was in a remote village with no electricity.      And then, of course, there was the farmer who tried to sell her a set of “authentic” tea leaves. She paid full price, and they were just regular leaves wrapped in a fancy paper.      That’s the thing about travel, isn’t it? You never know what you’re going to get. But I’m excited. I’ve never been to Nepal, and I’ve always wanted to see the mountains.      I still remember the first time I went to the countryside in England. I was in a village shop, and the only thing they had was sausages and bread. No gluten-free options, of course. I had to bring my own bread to the café.      That’s right. I used to work in a school, and I had a few kids with gluten allergies. I tried to make sure the school had enough alternatives. But it was always a bit of a struggle.      I’ve tried to do the same with my own kids. I even got a lunch box that’s gluten-free. It’s so much easier now with all the options, but it still feels like a hassle.      Yeah, I can see that. But it’s better than the old days, when we all had to eat what was on offer.

So, do you guys ever just feel like we’re all in this weird bubble of work and friendships? Like, everyone’s so busy with their jobs and stuff, yet we still manage to hang out all the time? I’m in admin, and I know it’s not the most exciting job in the world, but I like the routine. Plus, I think it’s kind of a good stepping stone for someone like me, who wants to move into something more hands-on eventually. Yeah, I get that. I ended up staying up until 2 a.m. to proofread the invitations. It was crazy, but I did it because I care about my friends. It’s not just about work, it’s about being there for people. That’s the thing, though. Even with all the stress and chaos, I think we’re lucky to have such a good group of friends. We might not be best friends with everyone, but we go out of our way to make time for each other.

So, do you know what’s going on with the library? I’ve been trying to get some info, but it’s all so confusing. Yeah, I know. I heard there’s a petition going around to save it from being demolished. I think the council is planning to turn it into a community centre or something. Oh no, that’s terrible. I mean, the library’s been a part of this community for years. That’s a good idea. I’ve been wanting to do something like that. Maybe we can start gathering signatures and spread the word through social media or even the local newspaper. Yeah, and if we get enough support, maybe the council will reconsider. I’ve heard that sometimes petitions can make a real difference. Although, I’m not sure how effective they are in the long run. I know, but it’s better than nothing. And it’s something we can do together. It’s not like we can just sit back and do nothing while our community’s resources disappear. True. I’ve also been thinking about my shifts at work lately. I’ve got this new job as an administrator, and the hours are really unpredictable. I mean, I’m used to a more structured schedule, and this is making it hard to manage everything. I can imagine. I’ve been trying to adjust too. I know it’s part of the job, but it’s exhausting. I’ve been reading up on brain training apps to help me stay focused. I heard they can improve memory and concentration. That’s interesting. I’ve heard about those apps too. I’ve been using one called Lumosity, but I haven’t seen much improvement yet. Maybe I should try something else. I’ve also been trying to come up with some mnemonics to help me remember things at work. Oh, I use mnemonics all the time. I even made one for my work shifts.

Well, I heard a bit of a row at the shops the other day about the Jehovah's Witnesses. One of the lads was shouting at them about the way they hand out their leaflets. Oh, I don’t like them myself. Always pestering people with their stuff. I mean, I understand they’re trying to spread the word, but it’s got to be a bit much, don’t you think? Yeah, I suppose, but they’re not the worst. I think it’s just the way they do it. I’ve had a few of their leaflets over the years, but I’ve never actually read one. I know what you mean. I’ve had one or two, but I just throw them away. It’s not that I’m against the religion, it’s more that I think they’re too pushy. Exactly. And I heard they even knock on doors in the middle of the night. That’s not right. I think it’s a bit harsh. I mean, they’re just trying to tell people about their beliefs. But maybe they should be a bit more respectful. Hmmm. I suppose there’s a line between proselytizing and being obnoxious. I’m not sure where it is, but I know when I’ve crossed it. Yeah, I reckon they’ve gone past it. I mean, we’ve all got our principles, but you’ve got to be careful how you go about trying to convert people. I think it’s all about respect. Whether you agree with their views or not, you’ve got to respect their right to share them. I can see that. But then again, I’ve seen what happens when people start giving their views too loudly. It can get a bit out of hand. I’ve always thought that if you’re going to share your beliefs, you should do it in a way that doesn’t annoy the rest of us. You know, just a bit of good-natured conversation. I’ve had a couple of conversations with them myself, actually. Not too bad, I must say. They’re polite enough, even if I don’t agree with their views. Well, I suppose it’s all about how you approach it. If you’re genuine and respectful, it’s more likely to work. Yeah, I think you’re right. But then again, I’ve had enough of people knocking on my door when I’m not expecting it.

So, do you think we've got enough logs for the winter? I've been meaning to check the stockpile, but I've been so busy with the new project at work. Honestly, I'm not sure. I think we might have to buy some more. The weather’s been so unpredictable lately, and the log burner isn't exactly the most efficient thing. Plus, I heard the price of logs has gone up again. Oh, I heard that too. And don’t forget, there's that new restaurant opening in the village. I’m sure they’ll be using some of those local logs for the fireplaces. Still, I do love a good log burner. It’s one of the few things that makes the house feel cosy in the winter. I agree. I still remember the days when we had a proper fireplace in the old house. It was a real family gathering point. Although, I suppose modern heating systems are much more convenient, even if they don’t have the same charm. Speaking of convenience, have you thought about outsourcing some of the work? I know it's a bit controversial, but I’ve been reading about some companies in India that do transcription and administrative tasks at a fraction of the cost. I’ve been considering it. It's not ideal – I mean, we do value the local workforce – but the budget is tight. Especially with the new school academies and all the changes in the education sector. I can see where you're coming from. But I also think there's a lot of value in local employment. You can’t ignore the impact it has on the community. Still, I suppose if it helps your budget, it might be worth exploring. And don’t forget the fudge. I had some from that antique shop last weekend. The owner was a bit of a character, but the fudge was amazing. It reminded me of the old days when we’d all gather around the fire and have a cup of tea after school. Yeah, that sounds like a good memory. I still remember my first day at school. The headmistress always had a special fudge on her desk. She was such a character, but you could tell she cared. That must have been her way of cheering everyone up. I mean, even now, when I think of the old school, I always think of her and the fudge.

I just can’t believe how much the property prices have gone up since I retired. I mean, I thought I’d be able to sell that old bungalow of mine and get something decent, but now it’s like trying to buy a house in London. You wouldn’t believe it, mate. I saw an advert for a place in King’s Lynn the other day, and it was like three times what I paid for my place in Costessey. I don’t even know if I’d be able to afford it now. It’s just so unfair, isn’t it? I mean, I’ve been a childminder for years, and I’ve always managed to save a bit, but now that the government keeps cutting benefits, you just feel like you’re not even in the game anymore. You can’t even afford to buy a house, let alone keep up with the cost of living. Yeah, I know. And with the taxes on property, it’s like the government is just taking more and more from the people who are already struggling. I mean, I used to think I’d be able to buy a small house in the countryside, but now it feels like it’s just out of reach. I tried to get a mortgage from the bank last year, and they said I didn’t qualify. I mean, I’ve got a decent pension, but they don’t seem to care. It’s like they’re just waiting for the next election to screw the retirees out of everything. That’s not even the worst part. I mean, what about the council? They’re charging more for bin collection now, and they’ve even started taxing people for recycling. I don’t even know what to do with my old TVs and gadgets anymore. It’s like every time you try to do something, there’s another fee involved. I know, I know. I just keep thinking about how things used to be. When I was younger, you could save a few hundred a month and buy a house within five years. Now, it’s like you have to wait until you’re 80 to afford one. I’ve been thinking about going back to work, but I don’t know what I’d do. I go out with my mates, we get a few drinks, and it’s just like, "What’s the point?"

So, do you know what you're going to do when you leave school? I mean, like, what's your plan? Honestly, I'm still figuring it out. So, do you think we've got enough time to get to the slopes before the lift closes? I know it’s got to be packed with people after lunch. Honestly, I think we might be too late.
